slot.brief: A string fixed at both ends vibrating in a given harmonic; ask how the frequency changes when tension and vibrating length are both altered by given factors.

stem: A string fixed at both ends vibrates in its second harmonic at a frequency of $240\text{ Hz}$. If the tension is increased by a factor of $9$ and the vibrating length is doubled (keeping the linear mass density constant), the frequency of the second harmonic becomes:

verdicts.working: Second harmonic: f2 = (2/(2L))√(T/μ) = (1/L)√(T/μ). T→9T gives factor √9=3; L→2L gives factor 1/2. New f2 = 240×3/2 = 360 Hz.

working:
The frequency of the $n$-th harmonic of a string of length $L$ fixed at both ends under tension $T$ is given by:
$$f_n = \dfrac{n}{2L}\sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}$$

For the second harmonic ($n = 2$):
$$f = \dfrac{2}{2L}\sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}} = 240\text{ Hz}$$

When the tension is increased to $T' = 9T$ and the length is changed to $L' = 2L$, the new frequency in the same harmonic mode ($n = 2$) is:
$$f' = \dfrac{2}{2L'}\sqrt{\dfrac{T'}{\mu}} = \dfrac{2}{2(2L)}\sqrt{\dfrac{9T}{\mu}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{9}}{2}\left(\dfrac{2}{2L}\sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}\right) = \dfrac{3}{2}f$$

Substituting $f = 240\text{ Hz}$:
$$f' = \dfrac{3}{2} \times 240\text{ Hz} = 360\text{ Hz}$$

Independent check: Second harmonic: f2 = (2/(2L))√(T/μ) = (1/L)√(T/μ). T→9T gives factor √9=3; L→2L gives factor 1/2. New f2 = 240×3/2 = 360 Hz.
